value.overview: The Siberian Pipit is a slender ground-walking songbird of open country. Field recognition often comes from slender shape, streaked brown plumage, tail-bobbing, and open-ground walking. It is found on tundra, short grass, shorelines, agricultural fields, wet flats, migration fields, and open ground. In Canada, its status can be common, local, seasonal, or rare depending on the province and season, so current sightings remain important for trip planning.
value.classification: The Siberian Pipit (Anthus japonicus) belongs to the family Wagtails and Pipits in the order Passeriformes. This is the practical birding classification for quick field reference.
value.identification: Look for slender shape, streaked brown plumage, tail-bobbing, and open-ground walking. Also use size, posture, bill shape, flight style, voice, habitat, and season. Plumage can vary by sex, age, molt, and light, so the safest identification comes from combining several field marks rather than relying on one color or feature.
value.rangeHabitat: It is usually found in open ground such as tundra, shorelines, short grass, agricultural fields, and migration flats. In Canada, pipits are best placed by season because several are migrants or rare visitors.
value.migrationStatus: Migratory, with some species occurring mainly during passage or as rare visitors in Canada.
value.breeding: It usually nests on the ground in open vegetation, often in tundra, grass, or low cover. The nest is concealed, and young are fed insects and other small invertebrates.
value.dietFeeding: It eats insects, larvae, small invertebrates, and some seeds. It walks on open ground, picking food from soil, mud, grass, or shoreline edges.
value.behavior: It walks or runs rather than hopping, often bobbing the tail. When flushed it gives thin call notes and may fly in a loose, undulating pattern.
